title: Turning Fails into Features: Zapier’s Hard-Won Eval Lessons — Rafal Willinski, Vitor Balocco, Zapier

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 97%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is evaluation methodology, including eval hierarchies, LLM-as-a-judge rubrics, trajectory evals, and AB testing for AI agents. Zapier Agents is a general automation platform, and the evaluation lessons apply broadly across enterprise workflow automation. The talk covers the post-deployment cycle of shipping, collecting feedback, building evals, monitoring production quality, and iterating. Requires familiarity with AI agent architecture, software testing pyramids, and tracing/observability tools like Braintrust. Recorded at the AI Engineer World's Fair in San Francisco. All evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript.

summary: The talk covers Zapier's approach to building and evaluating AI agents. After introducing Zapier Agents and the challenges of probabilistic software, the speakers describe a data flywheel: ship, collect feedback, understand failures, build evals and features, improve, and repeat. Instrumentation should capture tool calls, errors, and pre/post-processing in runtime shape so traces become replayable evals. Explicit feedback is high-signal but rare; placing feedback prompts at critical moments like after test runs boosts submissions. Implicit signals—turning on agents, copying responses, rephrasing, frustration—are more abundant and can be clustered with LLMs to form an automatic roadmap. Internal vibe-coded LLM ops tooling pays dividends by enabling one-click conversion of failures into evals. The speakers present an eval hierarchy: unit-test evals at the base for debugging specific failures, trajectory evals in the middle for multi-turn criteria, and AB testing with staged rollouts at the top. They discovered that over-indexing on fine-grained unit-test evals made newer, stronger models appear worse because those evals were overfit to existing model behavior and penalized valid alternative paths. Reasoning models with Braintrust MCP helped surface meaningful differences between model runs, revealing Claude as a decisive executor and Gemini as more verbose and prone to hallucinating bad JSON. Trajectory evals grade entire runs including all tool calls and artifacts, but are harder to set up—especially with side-effecting tools—and can take up to an hour. Zapier chose not to mock environments, instead mirroring real user environments with synthetic copies. For LLM-as-a-judge, they use rubrics-based scoring with handcrafted per-row rubrics. They divide their eval dataset into a regressions pool (ensure existing use cases don't break) and an aspirational pool (extremely hard cases). Ultimately, the speakers stress that user satisfaction, not lab metrics, is the goal: when a good metric becomes a target, it ceases to be good, and the ultimate verification method is a small-traffic AB test monitoring real feedback and retention.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction to Zapier Agents and the challenge of building agentic products
sections.summary: Speakers introduce Zapier Agents as a more agentic alternative to Zapier's traditional automation. They emphasize that building good AI agents is hard, and building a platform for non-technical users to build agents is even harder, because both AI and users are non-deterministic. Prototyping with libraries like LangChain deceptively appears easy, but production probabilistic software requires a different mindset.

sections.title: The data flywheel concept
sections.summary: After shipping, responsibility shifts to building a data flywheel: collect feedback, understand usage patterns and failures, build evals and features, improve the product, attract more users, and repeat. This creates a continuous improvement loop.

sections.title: Instrumentation and tracing for eval reproducibility
sections.summary: Instrumentation should go beyond LLM completion calls to include tool calls, errors, and pre/post-processing steps. Logging data in the same shape as runtime makes it easy to convert traces into eval runs with prepopulated inputs and expected outputs, and to mock side effects from tool calls.

sections.title: Collecting explicit and implicit feedback
sections.summary: Explicit feedback is high-signal but rare; asking at critical moments (e.g., after a test run) boosts submissions. Implicit feedback is more abundant: turning on an agent, copying responses, rephrasing requests, expressing frustration, or cursing all serve as signals. LLMs can detect and group frustrations, though this requires tinkering. Traditional metrics like churn can also reveal implicit signal.

sections.title: LLM ops tooling and understanding failures at scale
sections.summary: Speakers advocate buying or building LLM ops software. Vibe-coding internal tooling with Cursor and Claude Code pays dividends by enabling domain-specific understanding and one-click conversion of failures into evals. At scale, clustering and bucketing failure modes creates an automatic roadmap. Reasoning models can also help explain failures by analyzing traces.

sections.title: Eval hierarchy: unit tests, trajectory evals, and AB testing
sections.summary: Evals can be organized in a testing-pyramid-like hierarchy: unit-test evals at the base (simple next-state assertions), trajectory/end-to-end evals in the middle, and AB testing with staged rollouts at the top. They recommend starting with unit-test evals but warn against turning every positive feedback into an eval; unit-test evals are best for hill-climbing specific failure modes.

sections.title: Over-indexing on unit-test evals and using reasoning models for comparison
sections.summary: They discovered they had over-indexed on fine-grained unit-test evals, which created noise that made newer stronger models appear worse in benchmarks. Using a reasoning model with Braintrust MCP, they could compare runs (e.g., Gemini Pro vs Claude) and surface meaningful differences that were hard to spot manually.

sections.title: Reasoning model findings and trajectory evals in depth
sections.summary: The reasoning model comparison revealed Claude as a decisive executor and Gemini as verbose, asking follow-up questions, needing affirmations, and hallucinating bad JSON. This surfaced a core problem with unit-test evals: different models take different valid paths to the same goal, but unit-test evals hardcode one path and penalize alternatives, overfitting to existing models. They began experimenting with trajectory evals, grading entire runs including all tool calls and artifacts, not just one iteration or the end state.

sections.title: Trajectory eval challenges: side effects, mocking, and LLM-as-a-judge
sections.summary: Trajectory evals have high ROI but are harder to set up, especially with side-effecting tools (e.g., sending emails). Zapier chose not to mock environments, instead mirroring real user environments with synthetic copies. Trajectory evals can take up to an hour. For LLM-as-a-judge, they use rubrics-based scoring where each dataset row has handcrafted rubrics describing what the LLM should evaluate, such as whether the agent reacted to an unexpected calendar API error and retried.

sections.title: Mental model of eval types and closing thoughts
sections.summary: Their current mental model: LLM-as-a-judge/rubrics-based evals for high-level benchmarking of new models, trajectory evals for multi-turn criteria, and unit-test evals for debugging specific failures (beware overfitting). Closing thoughts: don't obsess over metrics (Goodhart's law); a 100% score means the dataset is uninteresting, not that the model is good. Divide datasets into regressions (don't break existing use cases) and aspirational (extremely hard) pools. The ultimate goal is user satisfaction, verified via small-traffic AB tests monitoring real feedback, activation, and retention.

demonstrations: Showing how users test an agent before turning it on as implicit positive feedback
Example of a user telling an agent to stop slinging around as implicit negative feedback
Using a reasoning LLM with Braintrust MCP to compare Gemini Pro vs Claude runs, finding Claude decisive and Gemini verbose
Rubrics-based scoring example: 'did the agent react to an unexpected error from the calendar API and then try it again'
limitations: Explicit feedback is rare; detailed and actionable explicit feedback is even harder to obtain
Unit-test evals are noisy, overfit to existing models, and penalize valid alternative paths
Using LLMs to detect and group frustrations required significant tinkering
Looking at aggregated traces manually is difficult—easy to understand a single trace but hard to see patterns across many
Trajectory evals are much harder to set up, especially with side-effecting tools, and can take up to an hour
LLM-as-a-judge can introduce subtle biases and ensuring correct judgment is surprisingly hard
A 100% eval score likely means the dataset is not interesting, not that the model is that good
quantitativeClaims: Showing a feedback call-to-action at the bottom after an agent finishes running gave a really nice bump in feedback submissions
Trajectory evals can sometimes take up to an hour
Recommend routing about 5% of traffic to a new model or prompt for AB testing
